author: Jim Lowe Staff Writer
title: Vermont's Champlain Trio: Intrepid threesome spreads the word | Rutland Reader | rutlandherald.com
text:
Five years ago, three professional Vermont musicians found themselves sidelined by the COVID pandemic, just like all the other American musicians. But this intrepid threesome was not to be stopped.
First, pianist Hiromi Fukuda, violinist Letitia Quante and cellist Emily Taubl, all Burlington area residents, decided to use the time to form a piano trio. But they went a step further — a big one.
The trio’s debut project, “Empty Stages: Performances and Stories of Resilience,” took the three to six concert halls around the state. The film of a performance by the trio was complemented by interviews with people either from the venue or the community, or both, who could relate how the COVID-19 pandemic has impacted them. Directed by renowned Barnet filmmaker Jay Craven, the films were presented on Vermont Public (and are available on the trio’s website).
“We wanted to do something as a trio that was something more than a prerecorded concert,” Taubl said at the time. “We came up with the idea to film at selected venues across the state and show just how beautiful the facilities are. Jay and his crew use(d) a drone so you really see every aspect of the facility. And then we play a short movement from the stage — obviously, to no one.
“The idea was first of all to support the venue through this awful time in any way we can,” Taubl said. “The second thing was to take this time to put them into the spotlight because Vermont has so many gems of halls all over the state.”
And, of course, the third reason was to introduce this ensemble to its home state — which has since welcomed its own piano trio with open arms.
The Champlain Trio, now entering its fifth season, will take its Fall Program to three Vermont communities: 2 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 12, Vermont State University in Lyndonville; 2 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 19, at the North Universalist Chapel Society in Woodstock; and 2 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 2, at Vermont State University’s Dibden Center in Johnson.
The program features: Bedřich Smetana’s Piano Trio in G minor, Op. 15; Charlotte Sohy’s 1931 Piano Trio in A minor, Op. 24; and “Soir et Matin” (1907) by Mel Bonis (Mélanie Hélène Bonis).
“We had a very busy spring season,” Fukuda said in a recent Zoom interview.
“We actually played only one concert in Vermont and everything else was in New York and Connecticut, so we visited a lot of new places, and that means a lot of new audiences. And that was really exciting.”
“Yeah, it was fun,” Quante added.
“And then, finally, we did the recording of the new album ‘Forgotten Voices’ in January and then, finally, photos and editing,” Fukuda said. “We released it fairly recently and so we are happy to have that out in the world.” (The CD is available on the trio’s website as well at the concerts.)
The Champlain Trio is just beginning its fall tour which, in addition to the Vermont dates, includes Keene, New York (Oct. 11) and Cold Spring, New York (Nov. 15).
“The first half is a selection from the album (Bonis and Sohy) since we’re trying to promote it,” Fukuda said. “And then we added Smetana to make it more interesting. It’s highly emotional, dramatic, big. We didn’t want to limit us to just female composers.”
Still, female composers play an important part of the Champlain Trio’s repertoire.
“The (Dora) Pejačević, for example, the emotional roller coaster that she goes on, it’s not a female emotional roller coaster,” Quante said. (They have released Pejačević’s Piano Trio in C Major, Op. 29, on its own CD).
“We had a lot of discussion about all the album, what to include,” Quante said. “We actually explored more than we put on the album.”
The Chaplain Trio is likely the most full-time chamber ensemble in the state. The VSO Jukebox Quartet and the TURNMusic Quartet only get together as needed.
“It’s kind of the center, you know,” Quante said. “There’s kind of an anchoring every week of finding the three of us, whether it’s discussing what’s going on in our lives or even balancing in our own brain. For me at least, I try to manage my energies correctly so that I can be fully happy with the music. And for me it’s a nice anchoring throughout my life.”
“We still rehearse every Tuesday and every Friday and sometimes extra,” Taubl said. “You realize you’ve done it for five years — five years — and I haven’t had a Tuesday morning to myself.”
“Everything works great,” Fukuda said. “It’s not like we have a concert, and then we backtrack, and fit four rehearsals in a row. We meet regularly so we have time to work on things and let it marinate a bit. And, honestly, it’s easier to fit that into our teaching careers as well because those are weekly, so we just save those spots for exclusively for trio.”
“It is rather full time actually,” Taubl said. “I won’t lie, we do it every day!”
